justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three time horizons, starting near 306.5 for the one-day forecast and rising gradually to around 310 at the one-month mark. The one-day estimate was anchored primarily by recent price action and short-term momentum, assuming no major overnight catalysts and a continuation of the prevailing trend. The slight upward drift in the weekly and monthly estimates reflects a baseline assumption of modest positive drift consistent with longer-run trend behavior, while acknowledging that mean reversion forces and macro headwinds could limit any rally. In other words, the central case is not a strong directional conviction but rather a mild continuation of whatever near-term momentum was present at the time of the forecast.

The confidence interval widths widen considerably as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 15 points, which captures normal intraday and overnight volatility. At one week, the interval widens to about 29 points, incorporating the possibility of a meaningful macro surprise, earnings release, or shift in sentiment within that window. By one month, the interval stretches to 56 points, acknowledging that a full month contains enough time for significant regime changes, policy shifts, or unexpected economic data to materially alter the trajectory.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals entirely. On the downside, a sharp deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected tightening move by a major central bank, geopolitical escalation, or a liquidity event in credit markets could easily break below the lower bounds. On the upside, a surprisingly strong economic print, a dovish policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices well above the upper bounds. These tail risks are real and by definition not fully captured within a 90% confidence interval, meaning roughly one in ten outcomes is expected to fall outside the range even under normal conditions, and fat-tailed financial distributions make extreme outcomes more likely than a normal distribution would suggest.
